senses: Linguistic purism.
ety: Borrowed from French protectionnisme, equivalent to protection + -ism.

senses: A Ukrainian folk dance.
ety: From Turkic languages: Turkish urgan (“lasso, tether”), Crimean Tatar arqan (“rope”).

senses: A person whose job is cleaning cesspools or sewers, or emptying privies by night.
A male night shift worker.
A nightwatchman; a guard who works at night.
ety: From night + -man.

senses: An animal, such as a dairy cow, kept for the milk it produces.
A person who milks.
A milking machine.
A conservative poker player who only raises the stakes on a good hand.
ety: From Middle English milkere, equivalent to milk + -er.
examples: The milker woke up at dawn each day to tend to the cows.
The snake milker massages the glands to extract the full measure of venom during each milking.

senses: A female ass or donkey; a jenny.
A small Spanish horse.
ety: From Late Middle English genet, from Old French genet, from Old Catalan genet or Old Spanish ginete (“small fast horse; light horseman”), from Andalusian Arabic زَنَاتِي (zanātī), the Zenati or Zenata Berbers, known as excellent horse breeders. Doublet of Zenati.

senses: rhea (large, flightless birds)
ety: From French nandou from Spanish ñandú from Paraguayan Guarani ñandu guasu.

senses: Sexual intercourse in general; sex.
ety: From Middle English fornicacioun, from Old French fornicacion, from Latin fornicātiō, from fornix (“brothel”).

senses: Of or in counterpoint.
With two or more independent melodic lines.
ety: From Latin punctus contra punctum (“note against note”).

senses: A person who or animal that secretes (emits a bodily fluid).
A person who secretes comparatively large quantities of blood-group antigens in their bodily fluids.
ety: From secrete + -or.

senses: The nucleus globosus.
ety: From Latin globulus.

senses: The methods or techniques used to teach adults; adult education.
ety: From andr- + -agogy, after German Andragogik.

senses: Capable of being, or appropriate to be, cited.
ety: From cite + -able.
examples: We file suggestions to correct the relevant Wikipedia entries, but are denied for lack of citable sources.

senses: Held as if in a trance; captivated.
ety: From trance + -ed.
examples: For an instant, the tranced boat's crew stood still.

senses: Clothing to be worn by a bride on her wedding day.
ety: From bridal + -wear.

senses: Trypanosoma brucei, a major human pathogen that causes sleeping sickness.
ety: Learned borrowing from translingual Trypanosoma. By surface analysis, trypano- + -some.

senses: The quality of being salubrious or invigorating.
ety: From salubr(ious) + -ity, from Middle English salubritē, from Old French salubrité, from Latin salūbritātem, accusative of salūbritās.

senses: A large cooking apple.
The tree on which large cooking apples grow.
ety: From Middle English costard, perhaps from Old French coste (“rib”) + -ard, in reference to its ribbed appearance.

senses: To become wise or wiser.
To make wise or wiser.
ety: From wise + -en.

senses: Having a glam style; glamorous.
Having the style of glam rock.
ety: From glam + -y.
examples: Heavy Metal, Music from the Motion Picture (1981, Elektra): This movie is pretty lousy if you're sober and/or an adult, and the soundtrack should be either glammier or skankier, or maybe both.

senses: A genre of polyphonic secular music mixing languages and dialects and nonsensical quodlibets.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish ensalada. Doublet of salad.

senses: Shaped like a rod.
ety: From rhabdo- + -oid.

senses: A mixture of methane and carbon dioxide, produced by anaerobic digestion of organic waste matter, used as a fuel.
ety: From bio- + gas.

senses: To slice, bone or make into fillets.
To apply, create, or specify a rounded or filled corner to.
ety: From Middle English filet, vylette, felet, filette, flette, from Old French filet, diminutive of fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

senses: The process of making an action of a higher animal reflexive.
ety: From automatize + -ation.

senses: A Japanese martial arts chain weapon that consists of a kama (the Japanese equivalent of a sickle), on a length of kusari (metal chain) with a heavy fundo (iron weight) at the end; a chain sickle.
ety: From Japanese 鎖鎌 (kusarigama).

senses: A flat bread roll topped with onion flakes. Instead of a hole like a bagel, it has a depression in the middle.
ety: From Yiddish ביאַלי (byali), from the Polish name of the city of Białystok.

senses: A level of administrative division used in Malaysia, Brunei, Indonesia, and Singapore.
ety: Borrowed from Malay mukim, from Arabic مُقِيم (muqīm, “resident”).

senses: A traditional drink from Galicia, Spain, made from aguardiente, herbs, lemon peel, coffee beans and cinnamon. It is set alight before drinking.
ety: From Galician, past participle of queimar (“to burn”).

senses: That can be embedded.
ety: From embed + -able.

senses: The former currency of Estonia, divided into 100 senti.
ety: From Estonian kroon (“crown”). Doublet of crown and corona.

senses: Having three axes.
Along all three axes
ety: From tri- + axial.

senses: A shaft in a multi-story building enclosing a stairway or staircase.
ety: From stair + well.

senses: A wild ox, Bos javanicus, found in Borneo, Malaysia and the Indochina peninsula.
ety: From Malay banteng.

senses: A sweet almond dessert pastry that originated in the Netherlands.
ety: Borrowed from Dutch banket.

senses: A type of magistrate in South Africa, abolished under the British in 1827.
ety: From South African Dutch landdrost, from land + drost.
examples: Remember the words of the young Bibault in the revolt against Van der Stel in 1706: ‘I shall not go. I am an Afrikaner and even if the landdrost kills me or puts me in jail I refuse to hold my tongue.’
About ten years before this resistance movement the settlement comprised merely four houses, one of which was used by the landdrost.

senses: One who kills a human being.
ety: From Middle English man-killer, equivalent to man + killer.
examples: Hence we may account not only for the grasshopper war of the Indians, but for the grasshopper duels among our midshipmen, military officers, members of Congress, and others who have been educated for mankillers.

senses: A non-SI unit of sedimentation rate (symbol S or Sv), the rate at which particles of a given size and shape travel to the bottom of a tube under centrifugal force.
ety: From Swedish Svedberg. Named after the Swedish chemist Theodor Svedberg (1884–1971).

senses: An entertainment at which a medley of dishes is set on at the same time; a buffet.
A French card game, somewhat like poker, but of earlier origin and involving different scoring of hands, played with a 40 card deck (four suits of Ace through 10).
ety: Borrowed from French ambigu.
examples: When straiten'd in your time, and servants few, You'd richly then compose an ambigu; Where first and second course, and your desert, All in one single table have their part.
Properly served, as is done daily in many a Creole home, an “Ambigu” may become an elegant and distinguished repast, though the viands are plain and simple.

In France during the following century primero became ambigu, and a little later another variation, called brag, sprang up in the west of England, from which poker is more directly descended in its American form.

senses: The capability of a product or system, to interact and function with others reciprocally.
ety: From interoperable + -ity; alternatively analyzed as inter- + operability.

senses: A fox hunter.
One who manages the hounds during a hunt.
ety: From hunt + -s- + -man.
